newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Bonds support firm start for Euromarkets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bonds support firm start for Euromarkets.

text.p: European financial markets opened firmer on Friday, finding support from solid performances by bonds and currencies but potentially likely to suffer a lack of direction from the absence of important data.
New York's Dow Jones Industrial average closed 8.5 points down on Thursday on weak U.S. durable goods orders, failing to give much leadership to Europe.
But London's FTSE 100 advanced in early trading on Friday, fuelled by sharp gains in the British pharmaceutical sector and a strong gilt and a steady to firm bond market, traders said.
By the middle of the morning the index was up 18 points at the day's high, with advancers leading decliners by a margin of more than five to three.
"As long as we get continual gearing from the bond and gilt markets, I think the FTSE can go forward," said one trader, who is targeting the 4,100 level by the end of the year.

Markets were taking some cognisance of some low-key U.S. data later on Friday, with the second quarter real domestic product figure due at 1230 GMT and Michigan September consumer confidence data due to 1400.

In Paris, French shares started higher, supported by a firm bond market, with stock market analysts saying the trend was bullish. "The market is still far from being technically overbought," said one.
The blue-chip CAC 40 index was up around five points by the middle of the morning.
Economist interpreted data showing French unemployment jumped to a record high in August of 12.6 percent as underlining the need for lower interest rates in France.
Trade remained robust with data showing France had a seasonally adjusted trade surplus in July of 11.10 billion francs ($2.16 billion) compared with a revised surplus in June of 9.78 billion.
Germany bucked the trend somewhat, with shares trading lower in early bourse dealings, hit by profit-taking ahead of the weekend after the DAX Index reached a new record high on Thursday.
The German debt market reversed losses but failed to help share market.
In currencies, the dollar bobbed along steadily in early Europe, clawing mild gains from the yen and awaiting its cue to push higher, traders and analysts said.
Market watchers said a happy confluence of factors were giving a bid tone to the U.S. currency.

"To the extent that the bond market is rallying in the U.S. that's going to support the currency and we're getting lots of good news in Europe as well -- all that paints quite a dollar-positive scenario," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in London.
A forceful performance by European currencies against the mark this week has helped lift the dollar, but analysts saw scope for profit-taking which could prove a mild drag.

Analysts said the U.S. GDP figures would be of limited interest because they were so out of date but warned that U.S. asset markets were currently hyper-sensitive to all kinds of data and so the dollar could be on its guard.

The markets are seen vulnerable in the run-up to the key non-farm payrolls figures next Friday, as they look to see whether the Federal Reserve was right in this week's decision not to raise interest rates.
Group of Seven (G7) finance ministers and central bankers meet on Saturday in Washington, where they and others are gathered for the 51st annual meeting of the IMF/World Bank.
While such meetings have had the currency markets on red alert in times past, little excitement is expected this time. CURRENCIES AT 0930 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.5223 marks and 110.63 yen by 0930 GMT, up slightly from late Thursday's European level of 1.5209 marks and 110.40 yen.
STOCK MARKETS AT 0930
LONDON - The Financial Times-Stock Exchange index of 100 leading British shares was up 18.3 points at 3,951.5.
PARIS - The CAC-40 share index was down 3.74 points at 2,107.8.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was down 5.89 points at 2.660.66. PRECIOUS METALS
Gold opened slightly firmer at $381 an ounce vs $380.10. Silver was three cents easier at 486 cents.
